los.text: Analyze the four stages of the business cycle.
Identify the three types of yield curves and how they reflect interest rates.
Identify fundamental economic principles, including the difference between monetary and fiscal policy.
Differentiate between inflation and deflation and how they are affected by the major economic indicators.

concepts.subtopic: Four stages, GDP, recession vs. depression
concepts.explanation: The business cycle is the recurring pattern of expansion and contraction measured by GDP and unemployment. Four stages: trough (bottom), expansion/recovery (rising sales, production, wages), peak (capacity reached, growth can't continue), contraction (decline from the peak). GDP = market value of all final goods and services produced within a country in a period, stated in constant (2012) dollars to remove inflation. A recession is a mild short-term contraction — by the Commerce Department definition, real GDP declining for two or more consecutive quarters; a depression is a decrease for six consecutive quarters. Expansion signs: rising demand, inflation, industrial production, stock markets, property values, GDP; falling unemployment and inventories. Peak: GDP growth slows, hiring slows, inflation rises. Contraction: bankruptcies and defaults rise, hours fall and unemployment rises, spending/construction/investment fall, stocks fall, inflation eases, inventories rise, GDP growth negative. Trough: GDP turns positive, unemployment high but overtime/temps rise, durable-goods and housing spending may pick up, inflation moderate or falling. CPI down but demand up = trough moving to expansion.
rules: Recession = 2+ consecutive quarters of falling real GDP; depression = 6.
Inventories rise in contraction, fall in expansion.
Inflation rises into the peak, falls in contraction.
misconceptions: Listing 'waves' as a business cycle stage.
Thinking unemployment falls during a contraction.

concepts.subtopic: Cyclical, countercyclical, growth, defensive industries; sector rotation
concepts.explanation: Cyclical industries track the cycle: durable goods (heavy machinery, autos) and raw materials (steel) — demand collapses in recession, best performers in recovery/expansion. Countercyclical industries move opposite (gold mining historically). Growth industries grow faster than the economy because of technology, new products or tastes (social media, bioengineering); companies retain earnings, so little or no dividends; they tend to react later, nearer the peak. Defensive industries are least affected: nondurable consumer goods — food, pharmaceuticals, tobacco, energy; fall less in bear markets, rise less in bull markets, lower risk and return. Sector rotation moves into defensives as the cycle peaks and heads into contraction. Fear a recession → drug companies, not biotech, steel or home builders.
rules: Recovery → cyclicals. Approaching peak/contraction → defensives.
Defensive = nondurables (food, drugs, tobacco, energy); cyclical = durables and raw materials.
examples: An investor fearing recession buys pharmaceutical stocks.
misconceptions: Calling biotech 'defensive' because it is health-related — it is a growth industry dependent on funding.

concepts.subtopic: Interest rates; normal, inverted, flat curves
concepts.explanation: An interest rate is the cost of borrowing, set by supply and demand for loanable funds, the borrower's credit quality, the term, and current/expected inflation; short-term rates reflect Fed policy, longer rates reflect inflation expectations. The nominal rate is the actual rate paid. When rates rise, older lower-coupon bonds fall in price until their yield matches the market (a 5% bond must drop to about $700 to yield 7.14% when new bonds pay 7%). The yield curve plots yields of one issuer (typically Treasuries from the 91-day bill to the 10- or 30-year) against maturity. Normal (positive, upward-sloping): long rates above short because lenders must be paid for time value of money, inflation's erosion of buying power, more default risk over time, and lost liquidity; occurs in expansions and predicts rising rates. Inverted (negative, downward-sloping): short rates above long, usually after the Fed tightens credit in an overheating economy — short rates spike (they are more Fed-sensitive); predicts rates will fall. Flat: short and long rates equal; no change in rates expected.
rules: Normal = upward (expansion, rates expected to rise). Inverted = downward (Fed tightened, rates expected to fall). Flat = no change expected.
Yield curve is built from one issuer across maturities — usually Treasuries.
misconceptions: Building a yield curve from different issuers with the same maturity — that is a yield spread, not a curve.

concepts.explanation: The yield spread (credit spread) is the difference in yield between bonds of the same maturity but different quality — commonly corporates vs. Treasuries. It widens when the economy sours (investors flee to the safety of Treasuries, so a widening corporate–government spread signals an expected recession) and narrows when conditions improve (investors sell governments for higher-yielding corporates, signaling expansion). The spread between the 2-year and 10-year Treasury is another popular sentiment gauge: narrows when investors are optimistic, widens when pessimistic.
rules: Widening corporate–Treasury spread → recession expected. Narrowing → expansion expected.
formulas: Yield spread = corporate yield − Treasury yield (same maturity)
misconceptions: Reading a widening spread as bullish.

concepts.subtopic: Who does what; schools of economics
concepts.explanation: Fiscal policy is government spending and taxation, set by the president and Congress through the budget (balanced when revenues equal spending; surplus when revenues exceed spending; deficit when spending exceeds revenues). Monetary policy is the central bank's control of money and credit, set by the Federal Reserve Board of Governors: expansionary/accommodative/easy when it increases money and credit, contractionary/restrictive/tight when it reduces them. The Fed has nothing to do with fiscal policy. Schools: Keynesian — government intervention; recover from recession by running deficits (lower taxes, more spending) to stimulate demand and employment. Classical/supply-side — lower taxes and less regulation increase the supply of goods at lower cost; supply creates demand through jobs and wages. Monetarist (Milton Friedman) — the money supply determines prices and activity: too many dollars chasing too few goods = inflation, too few = deflation.
rules: Fiscal = president + Congress (spending, taxes). Monetary = Fed (money supply, credit).
Keynes: deficits in recession. Supply-side: cut taxes/regulation. Monetarist: money supply.
misconceptions: Assigning tax policy to the Fed.

concepts.subtopic: Fed tools; federal funds rate; prime rate
concepts.explanation: Three Fed tools: (1) reserve requirements — raising the share of deposits banks must hold at the Fed shrinks lendable money and raises rates (the most drastic tool, rarely used); (2) the discount rate — what the Fed charges member banks to borrow; higher discourages borrowing and shrinks money supply (a managed rate set by the Fed); (3) open-market operations — the FOMC buys and sells Treasuries; buying adds reserves and expands the money supply, selling drains it; the most actively used tool. The federal funds rate — what member banks charge each other for overnight loans of $1 million+ — is a market rate, not set by the Fed, though heavily influenced; it is the most volatile rate and a barometer of short-term rate direction. The prime rate is the best rate large money-center banks charge their most creditworthy corporate borrowers; set by the banks (not the Fed), lowered when the Fed eases, raised when it tightens.
rules: Fed sets the discount rate; banks set prime; the market sets fed funds.
FOMC buys Treasuries → money supply up, rates down. Sells → money supply down, rates up.
Most drastic: reserve requirement. Most used: open-market operations.
misconceptions: Describing fed funds as the rate the Fed charges banks — that is the discount rate.

concepts.subtopic: Balance of payments, balance of trade, dollar strength, top-down vs. bottom-up
concepts.explanation: The balance of payments records all of a nation's transactions with other countries: money leaving the U.S. is a debit (imports, U.S. spending/investment/loans/aid abroad, dividends paid to foreigners); money arriving is a credit (exports, foreign spending and investment in the U.S., interest received from abroad). Its largest component is the balance of trade (exports vs. imports): a trade deficit (imports > exports) can devalue the currency over time; a surplus strengthens it. A weak dollar makes U.S. exports more competitive (good for exporters/producers → surplus); a strong dollar makes exports less competitive and imports cheaper (good for importers/consumers → deficit). Investing in foreign securities (e.g., ADRs) hedges a weakening dollar. Analysis styles: top-down starts with the overall economy, narrows to industry, then company; bottom-up starts with the company and broadens.
rules: Debits = money out; credits = money in.
Weak dollar → exports up → surplus. Strong dollar → imports up → deficit.
Reducing a payments deficit: fewer imports, more exports, fewer dividends paid abroad — not fewer foreign purchases of U.S. securities.
examples: More French perfume imported than bourbon exported → debit to the U.S. trade account.
misconceptions: Thinking a decrease in foreign purchases of U.S. securities shrinks the deficit — it reduces inflows and worsens it.

concepts.subtopic: Causes, effects on bonds, inertia, real income
concepts.explanation: Inflation is a general rise in prices (universally: a decrease in the value of the monetary unit), measured by indexes like the CPI. Mild inflation encourages growth; high inflation cuts buying power and demand. Causes: excessive demand (aggregate demand exceeds supply) and monetary expansion (money stock growing faster than the economy). Inflation inertia: inflation lags economic shocks by quarters; the inertial rate persists until a shock changes it — prices rarely fall because firms resist price cuts and workers resist wage cuts. Chain: inflation up → interest rates up → bond prices down, yields up; inflation down → the reverse. Real income rises when income grows faster than inflation. Deflation — a general decline in prices — is rare, occurs in severe recessions with rising unemployment, when demand falls far below supply or the money supply shrinks sharply; investors flee to Treasuries, which hold value or appreciate. A negative GDP generally signals deflation.
rules: Inflation ↑ → rates ↑ → bond prices ↓.
Causes: excess demand, monetary expansion.
Deflation safe haven: U.S. government securities.
misconceptions: Expecting unemployment to fall in a contraction.

concepts.subtopic: GDP components, employment, CPI/core CPI; leading, coincident, lagging indicators
concepts.explanation: GDP = personal consumption (largest) + government spending + gross private investment + foreign investment + net exports; imports exceeding exports subtract; net exports add. It counts output within U.S. borders regardless of who produces it — a firm's contribution is value added (sales minus imported parts). Employment indicators: average weekly initial unemployment claims and the average manufacturing workweek; ~4% unemployment ≈ full employment. CPI (Bureau of Labor Statistics, monthly) compares a basket of goods with a year earlier — the most used inflation measure; 'core CPI' excludes food and energy for their volatility (a media term). The Conference Board publishes three indicator groups monthly. Leading (predict 4–6 months ahead): money supply, building permits, initial jobless claims, manufacturing workweek, new orders for consumer goods and nondefense capital goods, supplier deliveries, 10-year Treasury minus fed funds spread, stock prices (S&P 500), consumer expectations. Coincident (move with the cycle): nonagricultural employment, personal income less transfers, industrial production, manufacturing and trade sales. Lagging (confirm 4–6 months after): duration of unemployment, consumer credit to income, inventories to sales, prime rate, CPI for services, commercial and industrial loans, labor cost per unit of output. A rising Help Wanted Index points to future wage inflation.
rules: Leading = where we're going; coincident = where we are; lagging = where we've been.
Stock prices and building permits lead; prime rate and unemployment duration lag; industrial production is coincident.
formulas: GDP contribution = sales − imported inputs (value added)
examples: Sales $60M with $16M imported parts → $44M contribution to U.S. GDP.
misconceptions: Classifying the prime rate or CPI as leading indicators — both lag.

lessons.title: The business cycle and which industries win where
lessons.objective: Name and characterize the four stages of the business cycle, define recession and depression, and match cyclical, countercyclical, growth and defensive industries to the cycle.

blocks.b:
Economic activity — measured by **GDP** and **unemployment** — expands and contracts in a repeating **business cycle** with four stages:
- **Trough** — the bottom.
- **Expansion (recovery)** — rising sales, manufacturing, wages.
- **Peak** — businesses hit productive capacity; growth can't continue.
- **Contraction** — decline from the peak.

**GDP** is the market value of all final goods and services produced within a country in a period, measured in constant (2012) dollars to strip out inflation.

A **recession** is a mild contraction — officially, real GDP falling for **two or more consecutive quarters**. A **depression**: GDP falling for **six consecutive quarters**.

rows: Inventories rise; bankruptcies, defaults; stocks fall
Durables and housing may pick up

blocks.b: The CPI is falling but consumer demand is rising. That combination — prices still soft, demand returning — is the move from trough to expansion. As demand keeps rising against fixed supply, prices will climb through the expansion to the peak.

- **Cyclical** — highly sensitive to the cycle: **durable goods** (heavy machinery, autos) and **raw materials** (steel). Demand dries up in recession; they are the **best performers in recovery**.
- **Countercyclical** — move against the cycle; **gold mining** is the classic.
- **Growth** — industries growing faster than the economy thanks to technology, new products or tastes (social media, bioengineering). They retain earnings, so **little or no dividends**; they tend to react **later**, nearer the peak.
- **Defensive** — least affected: **nondurable consumer goods** — food, pharmaceuticals, tobacco, energy. Fall less in bear markets, rise less in bull markets; lower risk, lower return.

**Sector rotation**: move into defensives when the cycle looks to be peaking.

Fear a recession? Buy **drug companies** — not biotech (funding dries up), steel (goes into cars nobody buys) or home builders.

lessons.title: Interest rates, yield curves and yield spreads
lessons.objective: Explain what sets interest rates, read normal, inverted and flat yield curves and what each predicts, and use the credit spread as an economic signal.

blocks.b:
An **interest rate** is the cost of borrowing: supply and demand for loanable funds, the borrower's **credit quality**, the **term**, and **current and expected inflation**. **Short-term rates track Fed policy**; longer rates track inflation expectations. The **nominal rate** is the actual rate paid.

Refresher from Unit 2: when new bonds pay 7%, nobody pays $1,000 for an old 5% bond; it drops to about $700 so that $50 ÷ $700 ≈ 7.14%.

A **yield curve** plots the yields of **one issuer** across maturities — usually Treasuries from the **91-day bill** out to the 10- or 30-year.

- **Normal (positive)** — slopes **up**; long rates exceed short. Lenders demand more for **time value of money**, **inflation's erosion of buying power**, more **default risk** over time, and **lost liquidity**. Seen in **expansions**; predicts **rising** rates.
- **Inverted (negative)** — slopes **down**; short rates exceed long. Happens after the **Fed tightens** credit in an overheating economy — short rates (Fed-sensitive) spike. Signals rates have risen fast and, most analysts say, will **fall**.
- **Flat** — short and long equal; **no change** in rates expected.

You must recognize each from its shape.

Riskier bonds yield more. The **yield spread** is the gap between bonds of the **same maturity but different quality** — classically **corporates vs. Treasuries**.
- Spread **widening** → investors are fleeing to Treasury safety → **recession expected**.
- Spread **narrowing** → investors sell governments for higher-yielding corporates → **expansion expected**.

The **2-year vs. 10-year Treasury** spread is another sentiment gauge: narrows with optimism, widens with pessimism.

lessons.title: Fiscal vs. monetary policy, the Fed's tools, and trade
lessons.objective: Separate fiscal from monetary policy and the schools of economics, list the Fed's three tools and the key rates, and analyze balance of payments, trade and currency effects.

blocks.h: Two policies, two sets of hands
blocks.b:
**Fiscal policy** = government **spending and taxation**, set by the **president and Congress** through the budget. Balanced when revenue = spending; **surplus** when revenue exceeds spending; **deficit** when spending exceeds revenue.

**Monetary policy** = the **Federal Reserve Board's** control of **money and credit**. **Expansionary** (accommodative, easy) when it increases money and credit; **contractionary** (restrictive, tight) when it reduces them. **The Fed has nothing to do with fiscal policy.**

Three schools:
- **Keynesian** — government intervention; cure recession with **deficits** (lower taxes, more spending) to lift demand and jobs.
- **Classical / supply-side** — **lower taxes and less regulation** increase supply at lower cost; supply creates demand through jobs and wages.
- **Monetarist** (Milton Friedman) — the **money supply** drives prices and activity: too many dollars chasing too few goods → inflation; too few → deflation.

blocks.h: The Fed's three tools and three rates
blocks.b:
- **Reserve requirements** — raise the share of deposits banks must park at the Fed → less to lend → money supply shrinks, rates rise. The **most drastic** tool.
- **Discount rate** — what the Fed **charges member banks** to borrow; raising it discourages borrowing. A **managed** rate set by the Fed.
- **Open-market operations** — the **FOMC** buys and sells Treasuries. **Buying** pays banks and raises their reserves → money supply **grows**; **selling** drains reserves → money supply **shrinks**. The **most frequently used** tool.

Rates to keep straight:
- **Federal funds rate** — what member banks charge **each other** for overnight loans of $1 million+. A **market** rate (not set by the Fed, though heavily influenced), the **most volatile**, a barometer of short-term rates.
- **Discount rate** — set by the Fed.
- **Prime rate** — the best rate big money-center banks charge their most creditworthy corporate customers. **Set by the banks**, not the Fed; falls when the Fed eases, rises when it tightens.

blocks.h: Balance of payments and the dollar
blocks.b:
The **balance of payments** records every transaction with the rest of the world. Money **leaving** the U.S. is a **debit**: imports, U.S. spending, investment, bank loans and aid abroad, dividends paid to foreign investors. Money **arriving** is a **credit**: exports, foreign spending and investment in the U.S., interest received from abroad. Debits exceeding credits = a **deficit**.

Its biggest piece is the **balance of trade** (exports vs. imports). A persistent **trade deficit** (imports > exports) tends to **devalue** the currency; a **surplus** strengthens it.

**Weak dollar** → U.S. exports are cheaper abroad → exports up, imports down → **surplus**; exporters and producers are happy. **Strong dollar** → exports less competitive, imports cheaper → **deficit**; importers and consumers are happy. To protect against a weakening dollar, own **foreign securities** (ADRs are the simplest route).

To shrink a payments deficit: import less, export more, pay fewer dividends abroad. A drop in **foreign purchases of U.S. securities** does the opposite — it cuts inflows.

Two analysis styles: **top-down** starts with the economy and narrows to industry then company; **bottom-up** starts with the company and broadens.

lessons.title: Inflation, deflation and the economic indicators
lessons.objective: Explain causes and effects of inflation and deflation, compute a firm's GDP contribution, define CPI and core CPI, and sort leading, coincident and lagging indicators.

blocks.b:
**Inflation** is a general rise in prices — universally, 'a decrease in the value of the monetary unit' — measured by the **CPI**. Mild inflation encourages investment; high inflation destroys buying power and demand. Causes: **excessive demand** (demand outruns supply) and **monetary expansion** (money stock growing faster than the economy).

**Inflation inertia**: inflation reacts to shocks with a lag of several quarters, and the inertial rate persists until something changes it — prices rarely fall because firms won't cut prices and workers won't take wage cuts.

The chain to remember: **inflation up → interest rates up → bond prices down (yields up)**. Inflation down → the reverse. **Real income** rises only when income grows faster than inflation.

**Deflation** — a general price decline — is rare, shows up in severe recessions with rising unemployment, when demand falls far below supply or the money supply shrinks sharply. Investors flee to **Treasuries**, which hold value or appreciate. A negative GDP is generally a sign of deflation.

**GDP** = personal consumption (**largest**) + government spending + gross private investment + foreign investment + **net exports**. Imports exceeding exports subtract; net exports add. GDP counts output **within U.S. borders** regardless of who produces it, so a firm's contribution is its **value added** — sales minus imported inputs. ($60M sales using $16M of Singapore parts → $44M.)

**Employment**: watch average weekly **initial unemployment claims** and the average **manufacturing workweek**; about **4%** unemployment ≈ full employment.

**CPI**: the Bureau of Labor Statistics' monthly comparison of a basket of goods with a year earlier — the standard inflation measure. **Core CPI** (a media term) strips out **food and energy** for their volatility.

The **Conference Board** publishes three groups monthly: where we're **going**, where we **are**, where we've **been**.

**Leading** (turn 4–6 months ahead): money supply; **building permits**; initial jobless claims; manufacturing workweek; new orders for consumer goods and nondefense capital goods; supplier deliveries; the **10-year Treasury minus fed funds** spread; **stock prices (S&P 500)**; consumer expectations.

**Coincident**: nonagricultural employment; personal income less transfers; **industrial production**; manufacturing and trade sales.

**Lagging** (confirm 4–6 months later): **duration of unemployment**; consumer credit to income; inventories to sales; the **prime rate**; **CPI for services**; commercial and industrial loans; labor cost per unit of output.

A rising **Help Wanted Index** means employers are hiring → competition for workers → future **wage inflation**.

questions.stem: Under the Commerce Department definition, the economy is in a recession when real GDP declines for at least
questions.explanation: A recession is two or more consecutive quarters of declining real GDP; six consecutive quarters is a depression.
why: One quarter does not meet the definition.

questions.stem: Economic data show rising inventories, increasing bankruptcies and bond defaults, falling stock prices and a decreasing inflation rate. The economy is most likely in
questions.explanation: Rising inventories (slackening demand), defaults, falling markets and easing inflation characterize the contraction phase.
why: Expansion features falling inventories and rising markets.
Peaks show slowing growth with rising inflation.
At the trough GDP growth turns positive.

questions.stem: The expansion phase of the business cycle is typically characterized by all of the following EXCEPT
questions.explanation: In an expansion inventories fall as demand outpaces production; rising inventories signal contraction.

questions.stem: An adviser believes the economy is about to peak and enter a contraction. Using sector rotation, she would most likely move client assets into
questions.explanation: Defensive industries — nondurable consumer goods such as food, drugs, tobacco and energy — hold up best in a downturn.
why: Steel is a cyclical raw material.
Social media is a growth industry.

questions.stem: Which type of industry tends to perform best during the recovery (expansion) stage of the business cycle?
questions.explanation: Cyclical industries (durables, raw materials) track the cycle and lead in recoveries; defensives are stable throughout; countercyclicals move the opposite way.
why: Countercyclicals (e.g., gold mining) tend to fall as the economy heats up.

questions.stem: Long-term interest rates normally exceed short-term rates because lenders must be compensated for all of the following EXCEPT
options: reduced purchasing power due to inflation.
greater default risk over longer periods.
Federal Reserve purchases of long-term bonds.
questions.explanation: The normal upward slope reflects time value, inflation, default risk over time and lost liquidity; Fed activity mainly influences short-term rates.

questions.stem: An analyst's plot of Treasury yields shows the 1-year rate at 5.2%, the 10-year at 4.4% and the 30-year at 4.1%. This yield curve is
options: flat, suggesting no change in rates.
inverted, typically following Fed tightening in an overheating economy.
questions.explanation: Short rates above long rates is an inverted (negative) curve, usually the product of a sharp rise in short rates from Fed tightening; most analysts expect rates to fall afterward.
why: A flat curve has equal rates across maturities.
Positive is another name for normal.

questions.stem: A yield curve is properly constructed by plotting
options: yields of bonds from many issuers with the same maturity.
yields of a single issuer's bonds across a range of maturities.
the difference between corporate and Treasury yields over time.
the federal funds rate against the prime rate.
questions.explanation: A yield curve shows one issuer — usually Treasuries from the 91-day bill outward — across maturities. Comparing issuers at one maturity measures a yield spread.

questions.stem: The yield spread between corporate bonds and Treasury bonds of the same maturity has been widening steadily. Most analysts would interpret this as a sign that
options: inflation is about to fall sharply.
questions.explanation: A widening credit spread shows investors fleeing to Treasury safety and demanding more to hold corporates — a recession signal. Narrowing spreads signal expansion.
why: Expansion is signaled by narrowing spreads.
Fed policy is not directly indicated by the credit spread.
The spread measures credit sentiment, not inflation.

questions.stem: Fiscal policy in the United States is determined by
questions.explanation: Fiscal policy — spending and taxation — is set through the budget process by the president and Congress. The Fed controls monetary policy only.
why: The Treasury executes but does not set fiscal policy.

questions.stem: An economist argues that the government should run a deficit — cutting taxes and increasing spending — to pull the economy out of recession. This view is most consistent with
questions.explanation: Keynes prescribed government deficits to stimulate demand and employment during recessions.
why: Monetarists focus on the money supply.
Supply-siders favor lower taxes and less regulation to boost supply, not deficit spending.
Classical economics is the supply-side school.

questions.stem: 'Too many dollars chasing too few goods leads to inflation' summarizes the view of
questions.explanation: Monetarists such as Milton Friedman hold that the money supply determines price levels and economic activity.
why: Keynesians emphasize government spending and demand.

questions.stem: Which statement about key U.S. interest rates is NOT true?
options: The discount rate is the rate the Fed charges member banks for loans.
The federal funds rate is the rate the Fed charges member banks for overnight loans.
The prime rate is set by large commercial banks for their most creditworthy corporate customers.
The federal funds rate is a market rate and the most volatile of these rates.
questions.explanation: The federal funds rate is what member banks charge each other for overnight loans of $1 million or more — a market rate, not a Fed-charged rate.
why: True — banks, not the Fed, set prime.

questions.stem: If the FOMC sells Treasury securities in the open market, the most likely result is
options: an increase in bank reserves and lower interest rates.
a decrease in the money supply and higher interest rates.
an increase in the money supply.
a reduction in the reserve requirement.
questions.explanation: Selling Treasuries pulls money out of bank reserves, shrinking the money supply and pushing rates up; buying does the opposite.
why: Reserve requirements are a separate tool.

questions.stem: The Federal Reserve's most frequently used tool of monetary policy is
questions.explanation: The FOMC's buying and selling of Treasuries is the most active tool; the reserve requirement is the most drastic; the Fed does not set prime.
why: The most drastic and least used tool.
Used, but less often than open-market operations.

questions.stem: Each of the following would reduce a U.S. balance of payments deficit EXCEPT
options: a decrease in purchases of U.S. securities by foreign investors.
a decrease in dividends paid by U.S. companies to foreign investors.
questions.explanation: Foreign purchases of U.S. securities are inflows (credits); fewer of them worsen the deficit. More exports, fewer imports and fewer dividends sent abroad all reduce it.
why: Dividends paid abroad are debits; fewer helps.

questions.stem: A weakening U.S. dollar would most likely
options: make U.S. exports more competitive and favor domestic producers.
make imports cheaper for U.S. consumers.
hurt U.S. companies that sell abroad.
questions.explanation: A weak dollar lowers the foreign price of U.S. goods, boosting exports and moving the trade balance toward surplus — good for exporters and producers.
why: A weak dollar makes imports more expensive.
Exports rise, imports fall — the deficit shrinks.
Exporters benefit from a weak dollar.

questions.stem: An analyst who begins by evaluating the overall economy, then narrows to promising industries, and finally selects specific companies is using
questions.explanation: Top-down analysis starts broad and narrows to the company; bottom-up starts with the company and widens.
why: Technical analysis studies price and volume patterns.
Sector rotation shifts among industries with the cycle.

questions.stem: If the rate of inflation rises, the most likely sequence of effects is
options: interest rates fall, bond prices rise, bond yields fall.
interest rates rise, bond prices fall, bond yields rise.
interest rates rise, bond prices rise, bond yields fall.
interest rates fall, bond prices fall, bond yields rise.
questions.explanation: Higher inflation drives rates up; existing bond prices fall and their yields rise. Falling inflation reverses the chain.

questions.stem: The two principal causes of inflation identified in economic theory are
options: trade surpluses and a strong dollar.
high reserve requirements and a high discount rate.
questions.explanation: Inflation results when aggregate demand exceeds supply and when the money stock grows faster than the economy.
why: Trade balances do not directly cause inflation.

questions.stem: During a period of deflation accompanying a severe recession, which asset class would investors most likely favor as a safe haven?
questions.explanation: In deflation, Treasuries hold their value and may appreciate as rates fall, while stocks, real estate and commodities tend to decline.

questions.stem: A U.S. manufacturer reports sales of $90 million, wages of $40 million, imported components of $25 million and net income of $15 million. Its contribution to U.S. GDP is
questions.explanation: GDP counts value added within U.S. borders: sales minus imported inputs = $90M − $25M = $65M.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a LAGGING economic indicator?
questions.explanation: The prime rate changes after the economy has turned, confirming the trend. Permits, stock prices and consumer expectations lead.

questions.stem: 'Core' inflation differs from headline CPI in that it
options: excludes food and energy prices because of their volatility.
is computed by the Federal Reserve rather than the BLS.
measures producer rather than consumer prices.
questions.explanation: Core CPI strips out food and energy, whose short-term swings distort the trend; it is a media term, not an official BLS designation.
why: Core CPI is still a consumer measure.

questions.stem: By far the largest component of U.S. gross domestic product is
questions.explanation: Personal consumption dominates GDP; government spending, investment, foreign investment and net exports make up the rest.
why: Net exports are a small (often negative) component.

questions.front: Four stages of the business cycle; recession vs. depression
questions.back: Trough → expansion → peak → contraction. Recession: ≥2 consecutive quarters of falling real GDP. Depression: 6 quarters.
Defensive: food, pharmaceuticals, tobacco, energy (nondurables). Cyclical: autos, heavy machinery, steel (durables/raw materials). Countercyclical: gold mining.

questions.front: Normal, inverted, flat yield curves — when and what they predict
questions.back: Normal (up): expansion, rates to rise. Inverted (down): after Fed tightening, rates to fall. Flat: no change expected.
Recession expected (flight to safety). Narrowing → expansion expected.

questions.front: Fiscal vs. monetary policy: who and what
questions.back: Fiscal: president + Congress; spending and taxation. Monetary: Federal Reserve; money supply and credit.

questions.front: Fed tools (most drastic / most used) and who sets discount, fed funds, prime
questions.back: Reserve requirement (most drastic), discount rate, open-market operations (most used). Discount: Fed. Fed funds: market (bank-to-bank overnight). Prime: banks.

questions.front: Weak dollar vs. strong dollar effects on trade
questions.back: Weak: exports up, imports down → surplus (producers win). Strong: exports down, imports up → deficit (consumers win).
Inflation ↑ → rates ↑ → bond prices ↓, yields ↑. Causes: excessive demand, monetary expansion. Deflation safe haven: Treasuries.

questions.front: Name three leading, two coincident, two lagging indicators
questions.back: Leading: building permits, stock prices, money supply, initial jobless claims. Coincident: industrial production, nonag employment. Lagging: prime rate, duration of unemployment, CPI for services.

terms.def: Record of all transactions with other countries; debits = money out, credits = money in.
CPI excluding food and energy (media term).
Rate the Fed charges member banks; a managed rate set by the Fed.
Market rate banks charge each other for overnight loans of $1M+; most volatile.
Government spending and taxation; president and Congress.
Inflation lags economic shocks by quarters and persists until a shock changes it.
Central bank control of money and credit; the Fed.
Best rate large banks charge top corporate borrowers; set by banks, not the Fed.
Yield difference between bonds of equal maturity but different quality; widens before recessions.
